lit: clinging tenderly, unable to let go

use.how: Mostly an adverbial with 地 before a verb of leaving (依依不舍地告别), or a predicate. Said of people at a goodbye, or of leaving a place one loves.

near.diff: 恋恋不舍 stresses clinging attachment and can be said of things or pleasures; 依依不舍 is the tender sadness of a goodbye.
舍不得 is everyday speech and also means unwilling to spend or give something up; 依依不舍 is only about parting.

cue: At the airport a grandmother keeps hugging her grandson, walks him to the gate, and waves long after he has gone through. How does she see him off?

ctx.s: 毕业那天，同学们{依依不舍}地互相告别。
ctx.en: On graduation day the classmates said goodbye to one another, none of them wanting to leave.

ctx.s: 奶奶站在门口，{依依不舍}地看着我们的车开远。
ctx.en: Grandma stood at the door, watching our car drive away, sorry to see us go.

ctx.s: 假期结束了，孩子们{依依不舍}地离开了外婆家。
ctx.en: When the holiday ended, the children left their grandmother's house with heavy hearts.

ctx.s: “你怎么还不走？”——“跟你们在一起太开心了，真有点{依依不舍}。”
ctx.en: "Why haven't you left yet?" "I've had such a good time with you all, I really don't want to go."

ctx.s: 搬家前，他在住了十年的老房子里走了一圈又一圈，{依依不舍}。
ctx.en: Before moving, he walked round and round the old flat he had lived in for ten years, unwilling to leave it.

ctx.s: 站台上，两人{依依不舍}，直到火车开动才松开手。
ctx.en: On the platform the two of them couldn't bear to part, and only let go of each other's hands when the train began to move.

bad.s: 他对钱{依依不舍}，从来不肯请客。
bad.en: (meant: he hates spending money and never treats anyone)
bad.why: It is about the sadness of parting from people or places, not about being unwilling to spend money.

bad.s: 她{依依不舍}地把垃圾扔进了垃圾桶。
bad.en: (meant: she threw the rubbish into the bin)
bad.why: It expresses fond reluctance at a parting; nobody feels that about rubbish, so the sentence sounds absurd.

lit: like a body and its shadow, never apart

use.how: Predicate or adverbial: 他们俩形影不离. Said of two people, or a person and a pet, who spend nearly all their time together, as a lasting habit.

near.diff: 如胶似漆 describes intense closeness, usually of lovers; 形影不离 just says they are always seen together, friends included.
寸步不离 is not leaving someone's side even a step, often to watch or guard them; 形影不离 is habitual companionship.

cue: Wherever you see Lily, her best friend Mia is right beside her: at lunch, in class, at the weekend, on holiday.

ctx.s: 她们俩从小学起就{形影不离}。
ctx.en: Those two have been inseparable since primary school.

ctx.s: 这只小狗跟主人{形影不离}，主人去哪儿它就去哪儿。
ctx.en: The puppy never leaves its owner; wherever the owner goes, it goes too.

ctx.s: 那对双胞胎上学、吃饭、写作业都在一起，真是{形影不离}。
ctx.en: The twins go to school, eat and do their homework together; they really are never apart.

ctx.s: 你们俩以前不是{形影不离}吗？怎么最近不说话了？
ctx.en: Weren't you two always together? Why aren't you speaking lately?

ctx.s: 刚结婚那几年，他们夫妻{形影不离}，连买菜都一起去。
ctx.en: In the first years of their marriage the couple did everything together, even the grocery shopping.

ctx.s: 大学四年，他和室友{形影不离}，毕业后却去了不同的城市。
ctx.en: For four years at university he and his roommate were inseparable, but after graduating they moved to different cities.

bad.s: 我们昨天开会时{形影不离}地坐了两个小时。
bad.en: (meant: we sat side by side for two hours at yesterday's meeting)
bad.why: It describes a lasting habit of always being together, not sitting next to someone on one occasion.

bad.s: 他每天都{形影不离}他的女朋友。
bad.en: (meant: he is with his girlfriend all the time)
bad.why: It takes no object: the companion must come before it, joined with a word for 'and' or 'with', as in: he and his girlfriend are inseparable.

mean: to share joys and hardships together
lit: to taste the sweet together and bear the bitter together

story.text: After the state of Yan was crushed by its neighbour Qi, King Zhao of Yan set out to rebuild it. He invited able men to his court, mourned the dead and cared for the bereaved, and shared the sweet and the bitter with his people for twenty-eight years, until Yan was rich and strong again.

use.how: Predicate, often with 和/跟……: 我们同甘共苦了二十年. Said with warmth of spouses, friends or teams who stood together through good and bad times.

near.diff: 患难与共 is standing together in danger or disaster; 同甘共苦 covers both the good times and the hard ones.

cue: An old couple ran a tiny noodle shop through years of poverty and later success, always side by side. How would you describe their marriage?

ctx.s: 他们夫妻{同甘共苦}，一起走过了三十年。
ctx.en: The couple have been through thick and thin together for thirty years.

ctx.s: 真正的朋友是能{同甘共苦}的人，不只是一起吃喝玩乐。
ctx.en: A true friend is someone who stands by you in good times and bad, not just someone to have fun with.

ctx.s: 创业那几年最苦，我们几个人{同甘共苦}，谁也没有离开。
ctx.en: The first years of the startup were the hardest; the few of us shared everything, good and bad, and nobody left.

ctx.s: 你愿意和我{同甘共苦}吗？我现在什么都没有。
ctx.en: Will you stand by me through good and bad? Right now I have nothing.

ctx.s: 老板在年会上说：“困难的时候大家跟我{同甘共苦}，现在赚钱了，人人有奖金。”
ctx.en: At the annual party the boss said: "You all stuck with me through the hard times; now that we're making money, everyone gets a bonus."

ctx.s: 当年{同甘共苦}的战友，如今头发都白了。
ctx.en: The comrades who once shared every hardship and joy now all have white hair.

bad.s: 我和新同事昨天{同甘共苦}地吃了一顿火锅。
bad.en: (meant: my new colleague and I shared a hotpot yesterday)
bad.why: It means sticking together through a long stretch of good and hard times, not sharing one meal.

bad.s: 他一个人{同甘共苦}，熬过了最难的日子。
bad.en: (meant: he got through the hardest days on his own)
bad.why: It needs people sharing with each other through good and bad; one person cannot do it alone.

lit: green plums and a bamboo horse: the toys of a little girl and boy playing together

story.text: In Li Bai's poem about Changgan, a young wife thinks of her husband far away. She remembers that when her hair was still cut short across her forehead, she was picking flowers by the gate, and he came riding a bamboo stick for a horse, circling round and playing with green plums. They grew up in the same lane, two small children with no suspicion of each other, and at fourteen she became his wife.

use.how: Usually 是青梅竹马 or attributive 青梅竹马的恋人. Said of a man and a woman who played together as small children, often a couple later on.

near.diff: 两小无猜 (from the same poem) stresses the innocent trust between the two children; 青梅竹马 names the childhood bond, often of a later couple.

cue: Two neighbours played house together in kindergarten, lost touch at school, and married in their late twenties. What were they to each other?

ctx.s: 他和妻子是{青梅竹马}，从小在一个院子里长大。
ctx.en: He and his wife were childhood sweethearts; they grew up in the same courtyard.

ctx.s: 你知道吗？经理和他太太是{青梅竹马}，幼儿园就认识了。
ctx.en: Did you know? The manager and his wife were childhood sweethearts; they met in kindergarten.

ctx.s: 他们俩{青梅竹马}，分开二十多年后终于结了婚。
ctx.en: The two had been sweethearts as children, and after more than twenty years apart they finally married.

ctx.s: 电视剧里，女主角最后嫁给了和她{青梅竹马}的邻居哥哥。
ctx.en: In the TV series the heroine ends up marrying the boy next door she grew up with.

ctx.s: 回到老家，他又想起了那个{青梅竹马}的女孩。
ctx.en: Back in his home town, he thought again of the girl he had grown up with as a child.

ctx.s: 很多人羡慕{青梅竹马}的感情，觉得这样的两个人最了解彼此。
ctx.en: Many people envy a love that began in childhood, feeling that such a couple know each other best.

bad.s: 我和我太太是在公司认识的，我们是{青梅竹马}。
bad.en: (meant: my wife and I are a close couple who met at work)
bad.why: It is only for two people who knew each other as small children; meeting as adults at work rules it out.

bad.s: 我和我弟弟是{青梅竹马}。
bad.en: (meant: my brother and I grew up together)
bad.why: It is said of a boy and a girl from different families, usually with romance in view; siblings simply grew up together.

mean: well matched in family background for marriage
lit: the gates match and the households correspond

use.how: Predicate or attributive: 两家门当户对 / 门当户对的婚姻. Said of two families or a couple, about their social and economic standing in marriage.

near.diff: 郎才女貌 praises a talented man and a beautiful woman as a fine couple; 门当户对 is about the families' standing, not the couple's qualities.

cue: A banker's daughter is marrying the son of a wealthy factory owner, and both sets of parents are pleased that the two families are on the same level.

ctx.s: 两家都是做生意的，算是{门当户对}。
ctx.en: Both families are in business, so they are a fair match.

ctx.s: 老一辈人找对象，最看重的就是{门当户对}。
ctx.en: When the older generation chose a spouse, what mattered most was that the families were of equal standing.

ctx.s: 她父母反对这门亲事，觉得两家不{门当户对}。
ctx.en: Her parents opposed the marriage, feeling the two families were not of the same standing.

ctx.s: “现在还讲究{门当户对}吗？”——“很多人嘴上不说，心里还是在意的。”
ctx.en: "Do people still care about matching family backgrounds?" "Many don't say so, but deep down they still do."

ctx.s: 他们俩出身差别很大，算不上{门当户对}，可结婚多年一直很幸福。
ctx.en: Their backgrounds were very different, hardly a matched pair of families, yet they have been happily married for years.

ctx.s: 有人认为{门当户对}的婚姻更稳定，因为双方的生活习惯相近。
ctx.en: Some believe marriages between families of similar standing are more stable, because the two sides live in similar ways.

bad.s: 他们俩都喜欢运动和看书，性格非常{门当户对}。
bad.en: (meant: they both like sport and reading and get on perfectly)
bad.why: It is about family background and social standing, not about shared personality or hobbies.

bad.s: 这件衬衫和这条裤子很{门当户对}。
bad.en: (meant: this shirt goes well with these trousers)
bad.why: It is about matching families in marriage, not about clothes or things that go well together.

mean: to break off a relationship completely
lit: one stroke of the knife and it falls in two

use.how: Usually 跟/和……一刀两断. Ending a relationship, a partnership or a habit decisively and for good; it sounds firm and often angry.

near.diff: 藕断丝连 is the opposite: still tied by threads after a break-up; 一刀两断 leaves no ties at all.

cue: After finding out her business partner had lied to her for years, she dissolved the company, blocked his number and never spoke to him again.

ctx.s: 她决定跟前男友{一刀两断}，删掉了他所有的联系方式。
ctx.en: She decided to cut off her ex completely and deleted all his contact details.

ctx.s: 既然已经分手了，就{一刀两断}吧，别再联系了。
ctx.en: Since you've broken up, make a clean break and stop contacting each other.

ctx.s: “我要和你{一刀两断}！”她气得摔门就走。
ctx.en: "I'm finished with you for good!" she shouted, slamming the door as she left.

ctx.s: 他发现合伙人骗了他，当场就和对方{一刀两断}。
ctx.en: When he found out his partner had cheated him, he broke with him on the spot.

ctx.s: 他下决心跟香烟{一刀两断}，把家里的烟全扔了。
ctx.en: He resolved to be done with cigarettes for good and threw out every pack in the house.

ctx.s: 公司宣布与那家违规的供应商{一刀两断}，不再有任何合作。
ctx.en: The company announced a complete break with the supplier that broke the rules, ending all cooperation.

bad.s: 她昨天终于{一刀两断}了男朋友。
bad.en: (meant: yesterday she finally broke up with her boyfriend)
bad.why: It takes no object: the other party must come before it, joined with a word for 'with', as in: she broke with her boyfriend.

bad.s: 我们先{一刀两断}一个月，冷静一下再说。
bad.en: (meant: let's take a month apart to cool down)
bad.why: It means a complete and final break, so it cannot describe a temporary separation.

lit: the wish of one side only

use.how: Predicate (只是一厢情愿) or adverbial (一厢情愿地认为). Says a hope or plan ignores what the other side wants or what is realistic; also unreturned love.

near.diff: 心甘情愿 is being fully willing yourself; 一厢情愿 is assuming others, or reality, will go along with your wish.
自作多情 is imagining someone has feelings for you; 一厢情愿 is any one-sided hope or plan.

cue: He has already planned the wedding in his head, but she has only spoken to him twice and already has a boyfriend.

ctx.s: 他喜欢她很多年，可惜只是{一厢情愿}。
ctx.en: He has loved her for years, but sadly it is all on his side.

ctx.s: 你以为老板会主动给你加薪？那只是你的{一厢情愿}。
ctx.en: You think the boss will give you a raise without being asked? That's just your wishful thinking.

ctx.s: 别{一厢情愿}了，对方根本没打算跟我们合作。
ctx.en: Stop kidding yourself; they never had any intention of working with us.

ctx.s: 父母{一厢情愿}地给孩子报了钢琴班，孩子却根本不喜欢。
ctx.en: The parents signed their child up for piano lessons assuming it would be welcome, but the child didn't like it at all.

ctx.s: 合作要双方都愿意，光我们这边积极，那只是{一厢情愿}。
ctx.en: A partnership needs both sides to want it; if only we are keen, it is just wishful thinking on our part.

ctx.s: 婚姻不是一个人{一厢情愿}就能维持的，需要两个人一起用心。
ctx.en: A marriage can't be held together by one person's wishes; it takes both people's effort.

bad.s: 他{一厢情愿}地帮我搬了家，一分钱都不要。
bad.en: (meant: he gladly helped me move house and wouldn't take a penny)
bad.why: It means a wish the other side does not share, never doing something gladly of one's own free will.

bad.s: 我们俩商量好了，{一厢情愿}地决定下个月结婚。
bad.en: (meant: we talked it over and both happily decided to marry next month)
bad.why: It means one-sided, so it cannot describe a decision both people agreed on.

mean: to put oneself in another's shoes
lit: to hold one's own heart up against another's

use.how: Often a clause on its own before the point (将心比心，你也不愿意这样), or after 要/学会. Urges empathy, or explains why one treats others kindly.

near.diff: 设身处地 is picturing yourself in another's situation to understand it; 将心比心 compares with how you would feel, usually to urge fairness.

cue: Your friend snaps at a delivery driver who arrives late in the pouring rain. You ask him how he would feel if he were the one getting soaked.

ctx.s: 做事要{将心比心}，别只想着自己。
ctx.en: Treat people as you'd want to be treated; don't think only of yourself.

ctx.s: {将心比心}，如果你是他，你也会生气的。
ctx.en: Put yourself in his place: if you were him, you'd be angry too.

ctx.s: 老师说：“同学们，{将心比心}，谁愿意被别人取笑呢？”
ctx.en: The teacher said: "Class, think how you'd feel. Who wants to be laughed at?"

ctx.s: 我当过服务员，所以{将心比心}，从不对服务员发脾气。
ctx.en: I used to be a waiter, so I know how it feels and never lose my temper with waiting staff.

ctx.s: 半夜敲邻居的门借东西，你{将心比心}想想，这合适吗？
ctx.en: Knocking on the neighbour's door at midnight to borrow something: imagine it were you, is that reasonable?

ctx.s: 遇到顾客投诉，客服要学会{将心比心}，先理解对方的着急。
ctx.en: When customers complain, service staff need to put themselves in the customer's shoes and first understand their worry.

bad.s: 我和她{将心比心}，很快就结婚了。
bad.en: (meant: we loved each other and soon got married)
bad.why: It is about judging another's feelings by your own, not about two hearts in love.

bad.s: 我们俩{将心比心}，看看谁的成绩更好。
bad.en: (meant: let's compare and see whose marks are better)
bad.why: The comparing is of feelings, to understand someone; it never means competing or comparing results.

mean: to suffer the results of one's own doing
lit: what you yourself did, you yourself receive

use.how: Predicate, often 真是自作自受 or 是自作自受. A blunt verdict that someone's trouble is their own fault; can be said of oneself ruefully.

near.diff: 咎由自取 is more formal and severe, for serious blame or punishment; 自作自受 is everyday and blunt.

cue: Your roommate cheated a classmate out of money, and now nobody in the dorm will speak to him. What do you mutter about his loneliness?

ctx.s: 他酒后开车，驾照被吊销了，这是{自作自受}。
ctx.en: He drove after drinking and lost his licence; he brought it on himself.

ctx.s: 谁让你在背后说别人坏话？现在大家都不理你，{自作自受}！
ctx.en: Who told you to badmouth people behind their backs? Now nobody will talk to you, and it's your own doing!

ctx.s: 我熬夜打游戏，结果考试时睡着了，真是{自作自受}。
ctx.en: I stayed up gaming and fell asleep in the exam; I brought it on myself.

ctx.s: “他被公司开除了。”——“他天天迟到早退，{自作自受}。”
ctx.en: "He got fired." "He came in late and left early every day. He asked for it."

ctx.s: 他总是骗人，现在没有人相信他了，这叫{自作自受}。
ctx.en: He was always lying, and now nobody believes him; that's what he gets.

ctx.s: 小说里那个贪心的商人最后破产了，读者都觉得他{自作自受}。
ctx.en: The greedy merchant in the novel goes bankrupt in the end, and readers all feel he got what he deserved.

bad.s: 他好好地走在人行道上，被一辆车撞了，真是{自作自受}。
bad.en: (meant: how awful, he was walking on the pavement and got hit by a car)
bad.why: It blames the person for their trouble; said of an innocent accident victim it sounds cruel.

bad.s: 她每天努力练琴，终于拿了冠军，这是{自作自受}。
bad.en: (meant: she practised every day and finally won, as she deserved)
bad.why: It is only for bad consequences of one's own folly, never for hard work paying off.

lit: private for oneself, profit for oneself

use.how: An adjective, as predicate or attributive: 他很自私自利 / 自私自利的人. A strong moral criticism of someone who always puts their own interest first.

near.diff: 损人利己 is actively harming others to benefit oneself; 自私自利 is caring only about oneself, whether or not others are harmed.

cue: Your housemate takes the biggest room, uses everyone's food and never cleans, but won't lift a finger when anyone else needs help.

ctx.s: 他从来不帮别人，太{自私自利}了。
ctx.en: He never helps anyone; he's far too selfish.

ctx.s: 我不喜欢跟{自私自利}的人做朋友。
ctx.en: I don't like being friends with selfish people.

ctx.s: 你只想着自己方便，怎么这么{自私自利}？
ctx.en: You only think about what's convenient for you. How can you be so selfish?

ctx.s: 地铁上他一个人占三个座位，这种{自私自利}的行为让人很反感。
ctx.en: He took up three seats on the metro by himself; that kind of selfish behaviour is really off-putting.

ctx.s: 小组作业他只做自己那部分，别人有困难也不管，大家都说他{自私自利}。
ctx.en: In group projects he only does his own part and ignores anyone who's struggling, so everyone says he's selfish.

ctx.s: 父母为孩子付出一切，孩子却只知道索取，变得越来越{自私自利}。
ctx.en: The parents gave the child everything, yet the child only ever takes and grows more and more selfish.

bad.s: 医生说你太累了，应该{自私自利}一点，多照顾自己。
bad.en: (meant: the doctor says you're exhausted and should put yourself first a bit)
bad.why: It is a harsh moral criticism, never kind advice to look after yourself.

bad.s: 他{自私自利}地把最后一块蛋糕让给了妹妹。
bad.en: (meant: he gave the last piece of cake to his sister)
bad.why: Giving the last piece away is the opposite of selfish, so the idiom contradicts the action.
